bp: An online travel platform is trying to sell hotel rooms, but it does not physically own the rooms and cannot always trust that its displayed stock is current. A hotel may still have vacant rooms, while the platform shows those room types as sold out because manual inventory updates arrive late. That gap creates a practical loss: travelers who would have booked are sent away or pushed toward weaker choices, and empty rooms remain unused. The tempting repair is to add inventory proactively, meaning the platform opens a room for booking before the hotel has explicitly refreshed the count. The paper asks whether that repair is actually good for the whole platform. A booking is not valuable if the hotel later refuses it, and a sale is not true growth if it only steals demand from another hotel on the same platform. The real object is therefore not a room count alone, but a decision about whether one added room creates new confirmed revenue.
wh: The hard part is that the platform is deciding under two layers of uncertainty. First, it must guess whether a room that appears sold out is probably still physically available. The abstract calls this a supply strike: the displayed shortage may be caused by slow updates rather than by real occupancy. Second, even if the room exists, the hotel may reject the booking because the platform acted before receiving a fresh update. There is also a marketplace problem. Hotels on the same platform compete for the same traveler. If adding inventory for hotel A simply diverts a traveler who would have booked hotel B, the platform may count a transaction while gaining little or no platform-wide revenue. Past data is misleading because the platform did not add inventory at random; it likely intervened in cases that already looked promising or scarce. That makes plain before-and-after comparison too optimistic.
naive: A smart beginner would build a rule such as: when a popular room type shows sold out, add one more room, then check whether bookings rise. This fails in three concrete ways. It treats displayed scarcity as true opportunity, even though some sold-out labels may reflect real lack of rooms. It ignores hotel acceptance, so it can create reservations that later collapse. Most importantly, it counts local sales rather than platform-wide uplift. If a traveler books the newly added room but would otherwise have booked a similar hotel on the same platform, the action moved revenue between hotels rather than creating new revenue. The rule also learns from chosen interventions, so it can mistake the platform's past selection habits for real causes.
ap: The paper's central move is to turn inventory addition into a cause-and-effect question: for each possible added room, estimate what would change for the whole platform if the platform adds it, compared with the otherwise similar world where it does not. CS2NET builds that estimate by combining three pieces of evidence. One piece describes room type scarcity, asking whether the apparent sold-out state is likely to hide real physical vacancies. A second piece describes hotel service engagement, asking whether the hotel is likely to honor the booking if the platform acts. A third piece corrects the comparison so the system does not simply reward cases that were already easier, more popular, or more likely to sell. The output is a platform-wide individual treatment effect: a per-inventory estimate of how much confirmed booking and revenue should be added by this action, after accounting for rejection and sales shifted from other hotels.
mech: The mechanism starts with a candidate inventory addition: a room type on an online travel platform appears sold out, yet the platform suspects the hotel may still have physical vacancy. The first module turns room-type and scarcity evidence into a compact description of availability pressure. In plain terms, it asks what the room type, hotel context, and sold-out pattern say about whether the platform is seeing a stale display rather than a truly empty hotel. The second module studies hotel service-engagement evidence. It asks whether this hotel tends to cooperate with platform-side inventory handling and whether a booking created this way is likely to become a confirmed booking rather than a rejected one. These two descriptions are then fed into the causal part of the system. That part compares the expected outcome under intervention, where the platform adds the inventory, with an estimated missing outcome under no intervention. Because the missing world cannot be observed for the same room at the same moment, the system must use comparable historical cases while correcting for the fact that past interventions were not chosen randomly. The scored output is not merely "will someone book this room?" It is closer to "how much extra platform revenue and confirmed booking volume should this specific addition create after subtracting bookings that would have happened elsewhere?" The platform can then prioritize additions with positive expected uplift.
math: The main mathematical idea is causal inference, which here means building a careful comparison between two worlds when only one can be observed. For a given inventory addition, the platform can observe what happened if it acted, or what happened if it did not act, but not both at the same time. The individual treatment effect is the estimated difference between those two worlds for one candidate action. Probability enters because true room availability, hotel acceptance, and future traveler behavior are uncertain; the system estimates chances from repeated cases rather than treating any signal as certain. The room-scarcity and service-engagement parts are learned descriptions: they compress many observed signs into quantities useful for the decision, while risking the loss of unusual details. The bias correction matters because the platform's historical actions are not neutral evidence. If managers previously added rooms mostly for attractive hotels, a simple model would credit the action for outcomes partly caused by hotel attractiveness. The math tries to compare like with like by accounting for the reasons an intervention was selected. There is also a ranking and resource-allocation idea: many possible additions compete for attention, and the platform needs a score that values true platform-wide gain rather than local booking volume. The central tradeoff is actionability versus assumption: the estimate is useful only if the correction captures the important reasons interventions and outcomes differ.
dots: This paper belongs naturally to the repo's causal-inference family because it asks what would change if the platform acted, not just what pattern predicts a booking. It is a sibling of marketing-subsidy and e-commerce layout papers that try to separate genuine added value from sales that would have happened anyway. It also connects to advertising and e-commerce work because the platform is allocating scarce commercial opportunity: rooms, traveler attention, hotel cooperation, and risk budget. The recurring conference ideas are probability, ranking, and causal comparison. Probability handles uncertain room availability and uncertain hotel acceptance. Ranking appears because not every possible room should be added; additions should be ordered by expected platform-wide lift. Causal comparison is the deeper move, because the platform wants to avoid confusing a visible transaction with a new transaction. The paper also touches service reliability, since a theoretically profitable room is harmful if the hotel rejects it and damages user trust.
ww: The mechanism should beat the naive rule because it splits one messy business question into the pieces that actually decide whether the action helps. A raw booking count mixes at least three forces: hidden physical availability, hotel willingness to confirm, and traveler substitution across hotels. CS2NET gives each force a place in the decision. The scarcity part reduces the chance of adding inventory where the sold-out label is real. The service-engagement part reduces the chance of selling a room the hotel will not honor. The causal part reduces the chance of celebrating shifted sales as new platform revenue. This works when the recorded platform data contains repeated patterns: similar room types produce similar scarcity clues, similar hotel service behavior predicts acceptance, and similar market situations reveal what no-intervention outcomes tend to look like. The online A/B test reported in the abstract is important because it checks the decision loop in deployment, where traveler substitution and hotel rejection actually happen. The reason is not that a named network is powerful; it is that the score is aimed at the right target: confirmed platform-wide uplift.
po: The payoff is an operational rule for adding travel inventory without treating every apparent shortage as an opportunity. The platform can choose candidate additions that are likely to be physically available, likely to be accepted by hotels, and likely to increase total platform revenue rather than merely reshuffle demand. The abstract reports extensive experiments and an online A/B test on a major online travel platform, with significant increases in confirmed bookings and platform revenue. It also reports more than 10 million RMB in additional annual gross merchandise value and releases a causality dataset for third-party inventory management.
limits: Several assumptions must hold. The logged data must contain enough room-type, scarcity, hotel-service, and outcome evidence to estimate the missing no-intervention world. The correction for selection bias must cover the major reasons the platform chose past interventions; an unrecorded factor, such as a hotel manager's private constraint, could still distort the estimate. The method also assumes traveler substitution can be measured well enough to distinguish new platform revenue from shifted hotel revenue. The abstract reports a major-platform A/B test, but it does not prove transfer to smaller platforms, different countries, unusual hotel contracts, seasonal shocks, or hotels that change behavior once they know the platform is proactively adding inventory.
